utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, would you please make the solemn declaration in the document which the court usher has handed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please. Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The doctor has asked me to point out a mistake in the English translation of her original report. It's a minor one but it is one that would leave the report open for misinterpretation. It is on page 1 of the report. And it is under the section entitled, "The opinion is based on..." And it's the third paragraph, the number 3. In that paragraph. And the mistake is, she interviewed the accused in detention unit 3 or Scheveningen 3, not on the 3rd. She only interviewed the accused on the 11th and 12th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, doctor, I'd ask you to tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: My name is Vera Folnegovic-Smalc.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You can remain seated.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Oh, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, we are going to begin by discussing briefly your background, and I would ask maybe the usher to assist the doctor. Some of this has been summarised on sheets of paper on the ELMO. I would just ask the usher to help the doctor orient them on the ELMO properly. Doctor, I'd ask you to begin by describing for us briefly your educational background.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: I graduated from the school of medicine, University of Zagreb, in 1968. And by doing so, I gained a title of a general practitioner. After that for some time I worked as a general practitioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think perhaps you could go a little bit slower we won't wear out the interpreters this morning.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Thank you. So after that, I started my specialization in neuropsychiatry and I completed that training in 1975. And at that point, I obtained a title of neuropsychiatrist. Shortly thereafter, I started post-graduate studies in psychiatric epidemiology and public health, and in 1977, I defended my masters thesis and became a master of science. During that entire time, I worked as a psychiatrist in the oldest Yugoslav psychiatric hospital, Vrapce. In 1983, I passed or defended my doctor's thesis in the area of psychopathology of schizophrenia, and by doing so, I became a doctor of science. In addition to that, I attended many trainings, out of which I believe it is important to say that as an associate of the World Health Organization from Geneva, from 1978 until 1985, I attended training on the use of measurement, instruments, in diagnosing psychiatric disorders in various centres in Europe, such as Geneva, Munich and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, in addition to or during the course of your career as a psychiatrist, have you also had several positions teaching psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: My teaching experience began in 1991, officially, although even prior to that, I worked as an assistant to my professors, who were my bosses at that time. But in 1991 and on, I started working as an assistant professor in three schools in Belgrade: One of them is the school for rehabilitation; the second one is the school of -- faculty of psychology, within the universities of Zagreb; and also at the faculty of medicine at the universities of Zagreb, where I've been working since 1990 as an assistant professor. And in 1991, when I became a tenured professor in all of those schools, I continued working there, but now as a tenured professor. For a while, I also worked as a visiting professor for psychiatry at the medical school in Rijeka, University of Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, can you briefly describe for us what publications, if any, you have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do we really need to have this given orally? Is there no list that we can just accept?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is a curriculum vitae, Your Honour, which if the Court wishes -- some of her experience is directly on point to some of the issues in this trial so I thought it might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If would certainly be good to have her tell us about those, but it's a fairly grim process going through any psychiatrist's list of published material because they publish an awful lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, she was just going to tell us the number and draw our attention to two that have a particular importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. If that's the way you're going to do it, that will help, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Also the sheets that are on the Elmo, I've made hard copies, if it's of assistance to the Court. I've provided them to the Court staff. I'd ask that they be furnished to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We have got them, thank you. This will save us from having to write notes, certainly thank you. That will be a very convenient document but you don't want that as an exhibit. This will only reflect her evidence, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a demonstrative aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you please summarise the number of articles that you have written and tell us about the important ones for the matter that you have been asked to engage yourself in, in this case?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Well, I've published more than 200 Articles in professional and scientific journals in former Yugoslavia, Croatia, Germany, Britain and U.S. What is of importance for this expertise, perhaps, is that for a long part of my life, I was involved in psychiatric epidemiology and psychopathology so I have a number of articles from that field and also psychiatric genetics. What is important is that I wrote ten chapters in various textbooks and scientific books and it is also important to say that I authored a chapter in the most recent European psychiatric textbook, and just to add in the end that the latest textbook in psychiatry in Croatia for that textbook, I wrote a chapter on forensic psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us the most significant professional organisations to which you belong?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Do you mean the institutions that I worked in or some other ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, professional organisations such as the Croatian psychiatric organisation.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: The professional organisations that I belong to, I listed only three. One is the Croatian psychiatric association, and I served for a second term as a chairman of that association. I'm also a board member of forensic psychiatric association and also a member of several international psychiatric associations, and several times, I attended and was an invited lecturer at psychiatric congresses, international ones. I do not belong to any non-professional organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I'd ask you to summarise for us the professional positions that you have held in psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: From 1975, until present time, I've been working as a general psychiatrist which means that my daily work includes work with patients. This takes place at the general emergency psychiatric ward. In addition to that, from 1976 until 1991, I worked as a forensic expert for Croatia and other republics of the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I'd ask to you describe for the Court what was the nature of your responsibilities as a forensic expert to the courts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: I was invited to various courts, and at that time I was a junior forensic expert, and in the beginning, I mostly worked for the municipality of Zagreb, which is where I live, but together with other experts, I was also invited to some courts in other parts of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you be called in the course of those duties to examine patients regarding their psychiatric condition for the court?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of my routine assignments during that entire time. I would examine the patients, examine all those aspects that were required of me and then finally give my opinion to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue, doctor.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: After 1991, I became psychiatric court expert in Croatia, and when Croatia gained its independence and after I became a tenured professor, I was appointed chief of forensic expertise at the Zagreb University in the area of psychiatry, and this is one of the strongest and most important institutions for forensic sciences in our country. I wrote a total of over 500 forensic opinions. Most of them were in the area of criminal law and about 50 of them in the area of civil law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, presently, is there a more senior or higher level expert in forensic psychiatry in Croatia than yourself?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: At this time, my position is such that I am chief psychiatric forensic expert, which means that there is nobody above me in Zagreb. There is a colleague of mine in Osijek who holds identical position to mine there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, at present, are you called from time to time to review the expert evaluation and opinions of other forensic psychiatric experts in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: My function is such that I am verifying reports of others, and based on our law, a court can ask for an opinion of one expert or an opinion of an institution, and if the Court disagrees with an opinion of either of them, then it can send a report to the University of Zagreb and then I am head of a committee which comprises three persons; I'm a chairman of that committee, that investigates and checks that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd ask you to tell us were you a biological psychiatrist beginning in 1978?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Biological psychiatry is something that I've been involved with for a long time. I am a general psychiatrist, but in addition to that, I have specific licences giving me an opportunity to get involved with biological psychiatry and I've been doing this since 1978, and very frequently, I have to give an expert opinion regarding pharmacotherapy therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is your present position?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: My present position is director of university department, a clinic for general forensic psychiatry and clinical electrophysiology at the medical school of the Zagreb University which is located in the psychiatric hospital, Vrapce.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, Doctor, regarding your background, I would like to ask you if you have conducted any research that is relevant to the issues that were raised in this case, and if so, would you please describe briefly what that research was?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Well, my master -- since I defended my master's thesis, I got involved in the psychiatric research, and I've listed only three articles here that have something to do with the expertise that we are discussing here today. First of all, that is a research of genetic components of exogenous psychosis. I worked in this research as a principal investigator for Croatia, and research was conducted under the auspices of Colombia University from New York. The chief professor from Columbia in charge of this is Markin [phoen]. The research is still ongoing but we have already published several articles in the American Psychiatric Journal regarding this research. Other two researches that are important involve research of functional psychosis, their genetic and epidemiological indicators.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now, Doctor, I'd ask you for the next few minutes to maybe describe for the Chamber some of the basic concepts that we need when we evaluate the remainder of your testimony. I would ask you to give us a simple basic definition of forensic psychiatry. What is the role of forensic psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Forensic psychiatry is one of subcategories in psychiatry which, in order to assist courts in solving their cases and issues, uses psychiatric methods and criteria and requires the expert to have additional training in judicial matters needed to solve such issues and problems. That specifically means that the expert needs to be trained and have knowledge in the area of criminal and civil law and give detailed answers to questions put to him such as, for example, accountability, necessary treatment, recommendations, procedural capacity, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, our primary interest here will be in the issue of accountability so I would ask you to give us a definition of accountability.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Accountability is an ability of a person to fulfil two requirements: First, to understand the consequences and meaning of its actions, and the second one is that the person is able to control its own actions, understand and being able to control them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, based on your experience as a forensic expert in the courts of the former Yugoslavia, did you translate the essential question that's posed to a forensic psychiatrist who is providing expertise or was providing expertise to the courts at that time?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. According to former Yugoslav laws, the definition of accountability read as follows: The person is accountable if it is able to understand the meaning of its actions and control and manage its actions. This is a verbatim translation of the provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, how many different levels of accountability existed under the law of the former Yugoslavia in the period of 1991-1992?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: In former Yugoslavia, a law in force divided accountability into the following four categories: The first category was that person was fully accountable; the second one that the person had diminished accountability but not significantly diminished; the third one was significantly diminished accountability; and the fourth category was incompetent

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about accountable, the first category. Can you please describe for us the criteria for determining that somebody is accountable and perhaps give us some examples of people who would be considered accountable for their actions despite some psychiatric condition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But not significantly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, this is the first category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's the second category that she's used. The first one was completely accountable. The second one was not...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Diminished but not significantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Diminished but not significantly, so the third one was significantly so the fourth one was incompetent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm asking her now to describe the first one, accountable, and the types of psychiatric conditions that the person could have but still be accountable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Fully accountable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't see that you were getting to that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please describe for us what is the criteria for determining that somebody is fully accountable?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: The main criteria for somebody to be fully accountable is that this person is able to fully understand the consequence of an act held responsible for, and in practice that means that that person does not have any psychological condition, which means that that person has a diagnosis of sine morbo psychico or that person can have a mild condition that only in a minor way influenced him in that he only to a minor degree could not understand his actions. That person can have a very minor psychological condition such as a mild or moderate depression, also alcoholism, but alcoholism where the person is not fully inebriated. So in order to say that somebody is fully accountable, we should know what the person is charged with, we should know the psychiatric anamnesis and know whether that person had any conditions and what state that person was in at the time when the act was committed. So we have to know the elements of that particular act and also psychological condition of the perpetrator. So these are the questions we have to answer for the Court. So the criteria is that there is no serious disorder in understanding and comprehending actions and controlling actions. And there are also some conditions that are listed that can fall into this category, and also, we can have a person that has absolutely no psychological condition. As a consequence, is that such person is considered to be accountable and can be held responsible for the act committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, let's move to the second category, diminished but not significantly. Can you please describe for us what is the criteria that a forensic psychiatrist would use in evaluating that somebody is of that category?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: So the second category, category B, includes persons that can understand the meaning of the act committed by them but there are certain circumstances that reduce, in a minor degree, accountability. An example of that can be alcoholism, inebriation, certain degrees of retardation, dementia, post traumatic stress disorder, and similar conditions. Persons that fall within that diagnostic category are responsible for the act they were charged with but there is a recommendation that certain mitigative circumstances be taken into account when passing a sentence for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, let's move to the third category. What is the criteria for determining that somebody is significantly diminished in their capacity?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: When we say that a person is of significantly diminished accountability, we enter into a new group of persons, persons who can have a real mental illness, but at the time of the commission of the crime, the person is in a state of remission. This group would include manic patients, seriously retarded patients, demented patients, and a typical example of persons with significantly diminished accountability would be a psychotic patient who commits a crime which does not fall within the scope of his pathology. For example, if we have a schizophrenic person whose pathology consists in having feelings of being persecuted, of someone trying to kill them, and that person has no money and wants to order a drink and goes and steals money from another person, not the person they imagine is trying to kill them, that would be a psychotic person but the crime is such that is -- that the content of the crime is not directly connected to the content of the psychosis, and the consequences of this degree of accountability would be that the person is not accountable and then the psychiatrist has to make a recommendation to the Court as to what sort of treatment is recommended for that person. The person must be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor I'd ask you, could you define for us what is meant by a life psychosis?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: This is a very important term. Life psychosis is an illness which starts at a certain point and is likely to last throughout the person's lifetime. If it does not last throughout his lifetime because of treatment, then certain symptoms can still be seen. Alcoholism would fall into this group, mental retardation also, because once a person has been diagnosed as mentally retarded, every psychiatrist throughout that person's life will be able to confirm that diagnoses. Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, dementia and a number of other psychiatric diagnoses fall within this group. This is very important because if we are conducting a forensic examination of a person today and this refers to a period of many years ago, we are able to deduce whether the illness existed at the time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you now to move to the fourth category of fully incompetent or unaccountable for one's actions criminally. What is the criteria to assess or to determine that somebody falls into that category?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: The fourth category is the simplest one for psychiatrists. It is much easier to say that someone is suffering from a certain disease than to prove that he has not suffered from it. This means that a person is unable to understand what a certain act means and in that case, these persons are mostly acutely psychotic. For example, acute schizophrenia, delirium, patients with epilepsy who were having a seizure at the time, deeply demented patients and deeply agoraphobic patients. These persons are not responsible for the acts they are charged with under Yugoslav law, and they are never pronounced guilty. The crime they are charged with is listed and they have to have mandatory treatment in psychiatric wards which have special security. An amendment to the law says that the psychiatrist in charge has to send a report twice a year so that, in consultation with the court, the location and treatment of each individual case can be determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does that person remain in that facility until such time as psychiatric experts determine that the person is in sufficient remission that they may be released from that facility?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And when such a person is released, the person still has to go -- undergo treatment even when at liberty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I wonder if I could just ascertain where one particular category, where one particular condition falls into which of the first or second categories. Have you finished with the categories?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I was going to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This might be the best time to ask. Doctor, what about somebody who is intoxicated, who knows very well what they are doing, the character of what they are doing, and they are able to control themselves but by reason of the intoxication they do something which, had they not been intoxicated, they would not have thought of doing? In other words, the bravado that the drunk sometimes has, into which of the first or second categories would you say that that falls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard to say if I do not know what act the person is charged with and how foreign that act is to that person. But that person would fall either into category one or two. These are the two categories that satisfy the criteria for alcoholism, both as a general diagnosis and in a specific case. As a rule, we always produce an opinion for a particular crime. Then we talk to the person, we see how far they are able to talk about it, what effects this has on them, and, of course, the person has to accept the fact that they committed this and they have to be able to talk about it. So all I can say is that it would fall either under category one or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well let us take a crime committed by somebody who is, when sober, nonviolent, but when intoxicated is so inflamed by the intoxication that he commits an act of violence, and let's make it serious violence. Into which category would that fall? Are you able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If, for example, -- and I'm speaking now in accordance with Yugoslav law, if someone does not expect to be aggressive or maybe expects to be aggressive when drunk and then they get drunk and they drive and they kill someone, they are held fully accountable. So the fact that they were drunk is not seen as a mitigating circumstance. However, if someone commits another sort of crime, I would tend to place them in category two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Driving offences may arise simply because, by reason of the intoxication, he didn't see somebody or thoughts he could make it through the intersection in time. I'm thinking of something more deliberately violent. You'd say that would go into the second category?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. The distinction between the categories is not always easy to find and that's why I put that particular category. Not necessarily because it results from anything happening in this case but it does explain it, at least to me, a little better.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, maybe just to follow up on His Honour's question. Can you give us an example or illustrate for us a person who was charged with committing a very serious or very violent act, can you give us the level of intoxication that you would have to find in that patient before that person would be determined to be in the second category, diminished but not significantly?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: The person would have to be drunk. We have subcategories: tipsy, drunk and seriously intoxicated. For someone to be drunk, the alcohol level would have to be above 1. In most cases, that person would be placed in category two. If I may add, these are not mathematically precise tables so we cannot automatically place a person in one category or another. This is why expert opinion is made separately for each person. But alcoholism does not go beyond categories one and two. So this is the scope of the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would a person -- would you expect that a person who is sufficiently intoxicated to be determined to be in category two, would you expect that that intoxication would be readily apparent to witnesses to the crime, witnesses that saw him at the time of the crime?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. Even lay persons would easily recognise someone who is drunk. They might not recognise someone who is tipsy but they would easily recognise someone who is drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Doctor, I'd like to ask you to -- can you please outline for us the primary psychiatric diagnoses and I'd ask you to begin with the old classifications used for psychiatric diagnoses.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Today there are several classification systems in psychiatry but I have listed here the traditional classification which is still used in forensic psychiatry today, and which has been retained because of the interests of forensic psychiatry because it is very pragmatic. This classification is dichotomous and it places all disorders into one of two categories; one of these is psychotic disorders and the other is non-psychotic disorders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you define for us the meaning of psychoses?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: To be psychotic means to be unable to test reality, not to have an insight into what is happening around us, which means that the patient cannot distinguish between his psychopathology, between his illness and the reality tested by us who are healthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you to describe for us the current classification system and I would ask you to begin with telling us what is endogenous psychoses?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Endogenous psychoses are psychoses for which we do not know the epidemiological factor. They are thought to be inherited. However, morphologically, there are no methods we can use to prove their existence. This would include schizophrenia, paranoid psychosis, affective psychosis, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which are either unipolar or bipolar so that they can lead to manic or depressed states, and these illnesses are considered to be serious psychiatric illnesses and they are a paradigm of true psychiatric illness. They are so-called life disorders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, doctor is there another name for endogenous psychoses?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Functional, functional psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And am I correct in understanding you that if a person has an endogenous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Endogenous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Endogenous psychoses, that there is no readily apparent or observable biological cause of that psychosis?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: We know that there is a biological disorder in the transmitters but we cannot see it. We recognise it through pharmacotherapy because we know, for example, that schizophrenia is a disease that is due to the increase in dopamine receptors but we cannot prove this because there are no technical methods for us to see that someone has schizophrenia. We recognise it by its symptoms, and when we do recognise it, we administer medicine that we have available and that we expect to help. However, magnetic resonance, for example, or a CT scan, will show nothing. An x-ray will show nothing. We do not have any diagnostic aids to show us so that we can say, "Ah-hah, this finding means that the person has schizophrenia."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, could you briefly describe for us what schizophrenia is?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. There are several categories. The most frequent one is the paranoid hallucinatory type, where the person is not aware of reality. They have their own life. They were drawn into themselves. They lose their affective expression. We say that their affects are flat. When something is sad, the person will not be sad. When something should cause happiness, the person will not be happy. In other words, the person is autistic and the sequence of thoughts is disrupted. It is disassociated, hard to follow. This is very important because a schizophrenic patient has disassociated thoughts as opposed to organic psychosis, where thoughts are incoherent, and I'm saying this because the word "incoherent" is often used. However, this is the case with organic schizophrenia. Then there are hallucinations, which are most frequently auditory although they may also be visual. The person, for example, if someone enters a room here and there are 50 of us, if I were a schizophrenic, I would think this person has entered the room because of me, in order to hurt me, so that the person thinks that everything that happens in the world is revolving around the person. So they not only have ideas of being persecuted, they also have ideas of being great. I have patients who think that they are the Empress Maria Teresa or people think they are Napoleon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is schizophrenia a life psychosis?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could schizophrenia in some cases be a basis for a finding that a person is significantly diminished or incompetent under Yugoslav law?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: A Schizophrenic person, in over 90 per cent of the cases, is totally incompetent, not accountable. Only in cases of good or partial remission can we say that accountability is significantly reduced, but we never find that patient in the first or second category of accountability.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us what is paranoid psychosis?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Paranoid psychosis is prognostically better. It does not destroy the personality to such an extent. There is no emotional destruction of the person, but the person is intensively preoccupied in a mad way. The person is always manic. The person may be able to function well, for example, to do a manual job well. But throughout this time, the person believes that someone is following him or her, that someone is going to harm him or her, and these persons are very prone to the commission of crimes. They retain their level of social activity longer and, as a rule, they do not have hallucinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Doctor, could somebody diagnosed with paranoid psychosis, could that be the basis of a finding by a forensic psychiatrist of significantly reduced accountability or incompetence?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. These two categories are possible. Most often, the person is incompetent but if they, for example, steal something from someone, that would mean that accountability was significantly reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, you've described for us that affective psychosis really has two sub categories: One is manic psychosis and one is depressed psychosis, and you also used the word bipolar and unipolar. Can I take from what you've said earlier that bipolar means that a person fluctuates between both manic psychosis and depressed psychosis?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And a person who is unipolar consistently just shows the symptoms of one of these two psychoses?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: That's correct. They also fluctuate but this is very rare, so bipolar is usually manic depressive. Unipolar manias are very rare. Unipolar depressions are relatively frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us the character or the primary characteristics of manic psychoses?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Manic psychosis is a situation in which a person appears to be infantile, very agitated in a psychomotor sense but very rarely are they aggressive. They are usually cheerful. They have escapist ideas. Each one of us here would be able to recognise them. If it's a woman, she would be wearing a lot of jewellery, bows, she would be -- have heavy makeup. She would be wearing very loud colours such as purple, orange or red. The appearance of these people as soon as they enter a room shows that they are not quite normal. They will kiss everyone, give profuse compliments which are often in bad taste. They do not concentrate on anything. Their attention is very scattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in certain instances, can manic psychosis be the basis for a finding of significantly diminished responsibility or incompetence?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes, for both categories. However, in psychiatry, these people are rarely sued because everyone sees that they are ill and what they do is usually not very serious; it's either petty theft or prostitution, soliciting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, depressed psychosis, can you give us the basic characteristics or definition of that psychosis?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: In depressive psychosis, the main symptom is loss of vital and other instincts. The persons seem deeply sad. They are slow psychomotorically. They do not have the capacity to do things. They have no interests in anything. They cannot enjoy things. They do not enjoy doing things they enjoyed before. They often sit very still, so that even a lay person can see that this is a person who is sad and who is ill. They may have an idea of guilt which is completely unfounded. They complain or rather they say that they have committed a big sin and this is not true. They are afraid that for this reason something will happen to them. They are often suicidal, and what is very important, lay people see them more as physically ill than as psychologically ill. Their activity is reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it true that a person who suffers from depressed psychoses could be found in certain circumstances to fall into the last three categories of accountability, accountable -- I'm sorry, diminished accountability but not significant, diminished accountability, significantly diminished accountability, and incompetence? Is it true that a person suffering from this psychosis could fall into those three categories?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true. Persons who are depressive very rarely commit crimes. In our experience in forensic psychiatry, we do not deal with them very often because they are not active; they commit crimes very rarely. I had only one case in my life, and that was when a suicidal mother jumped into the river Sava with her small child in her arms. That is the only patient of this type I have ever had in my forensic experience, and the mother was held not accountable at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So Doctor, what you are telling us is that somebody who suffers from depressed psychosis, it would be very rare for one of those people to commit a violent act against another human being; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. If depressive persons are aggressive, then we say that they turn their aggression in on themselves, not against other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I'd ask you to describe the next general category of psychosis, exogenous psychosis. Can you please give us a definition what that is?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Exogenous psychoses are psychoses where we can recognise and establish an external cause which led to the psychosis, and the further subclassification is based on the etiological factor that led to the psychosis. It is important to say that exogenous psychosis as a rule are not a life disorder, they are a response to the etiological factor causing them and they are divided into the following categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we go into those categories, there is one question I neglected to ask you regarding the endogenous psychoses. Would it be correct that all of the endogenous psychoses are life psychoses?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that as a forensic -- a competently trained forensic psychiatrist should be able to recognise that somebody has one of those or has suffered from that psychosis, even if it was 10 or 15 years prior to the day of examination?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue with exogenous psychoses.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Very important for us is the alcoholic psychosis because one of -- this is one of the psychoses that both my colleague and I mentioned in our written reports and in our testimony. This is a psychosis which is consistent with the organic psychosis in general, which means that the person does not test reality. It is confused, can have hallucinations, and that alcohol is considered to be an etiological factor that led to it. With such persons, accountability is not there. That means that that person is usually incompetent or the accountability can be significantly reduced. This type of psychosis is susceptible treatment. It starts usually in a very rough manner and it lasts up to six months. In some rare cases, some patients can go from alcoholic psychosis into real dementia, however, there is usually no dilemma posed here because we know that that was induced by long-term drinking and this led to psychosis which, in turn, led to dementia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said that a diagnosis of this could result in a person being determined to be -- have significantly diminished responsibility or incompetence. I'd like to follow that up and ask you, is that true if the person is suffering an acute phase of the psychosis at the time of the crime or the time the crime is committed? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not quite understand the meaning of your question. Did you want to know whether the person after a psychosis enters the phase of incompetency?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question. A person who has alcoholic psychoses, you said that that person may be determined to be significantly reduced or no accountability. My question is, is that only true if the person is suffering from acute alcoholic psychoses at the time of the crime?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me clarify this. This psychosis is an acute stage, but if it should turn into dementia, then that person is incompetent again and this is something that can be easily proven in a psychiatric way. Psychosis is a psychosis. As soon as it ends, the person returns back to normal or reduced accountability. Should the psychosis turn into dementia, then the person remains incompetent. However, it is very easily clinically recognisable. That kind of a person could not, for example, deduct seven from 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please move on to the next category of exogenous psychoses, delirium? Could you describe for us what that is?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Delirium is a state that I will describe in more detail because I believe, and this is something that I included in my report, that Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic suffered delirium. Delirium is a condition that can emerge after a number of consequences. It is usually induced by alcoholism where a person reduces input of alcohol and that kind of person can enter a state in which it has -- does not experience reality as it is. That person acts in a strange way, has hallucinations which are usually very important; they are very vivid, they are very dynamic hallucinations that confuse the patient who already has a disturbed perception of reality. And usually we describe this as a delirium state of consciousness. That person has no perception of reality. That person moves constantly, is very agitated, loses sleep or has disorders and sleep rhythm, and that is a very dangerous medical condition. It can be deadly if the person is not treated. That person is dehydrated, usually develops other disorders. This delirium state is recognised easily even by laymen. It can come about after either a cessation of drinking or can be induced by a severe medical illness, severe pain or surgery that an alcoholic undergoes. These are usually the factors that lead to a state of delirium.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, can I take from your answer that if there was a person present in the room with us now who was suffering from a state of delirium, even the lay people among us, that would be apparent to us, as well as to yourself, that the person is in a delirium state?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes, most definitely. This is one of the most easily recognised conditions in -- among psychiatric disorders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And according to Yugoslav law, under certain circumstances, could a person in a delirious state be found to be significantly reduced or have -- or be incompetent for the crime they were charged with?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: The fourth category is most frequent among such patients but even a third one is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could you please describe for us or give us a definition of reactive psychoses?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Reactive psychosis is a psychotic condition with a non-typical clinical picture and can be induced by some kind of intoxication. It can also be a consequence of another reason. For example, a person can take a medication, can confuse and take a wrong medication. We usually see this in suicide attempts, when people themselves select the medication they will take. It is quite rare, and in forensic psychiatry, we don't see this very often so this reactive psychosis is quite rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in certain circumstances that could be the basis for a finding of diminished responsibility, correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: No, no. Here we have significantly reduced accountability or incompetency because this reactive psychosis has a level of psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, could you please describe for us what would be described as post traumatic psychoses?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: I will say right away that this is a post psycho-traumatic psychosis, although it is called post traumatic psychosis. So let's not confuse it. This is psycho-traumatic. This is a result of a physical trauma to brain which can also be called wounding and leads to organic changes in the brain tissue, and this is when we call this post traumatic psychosis. In this case, it does not apply at all. It also leads either to a significantly reduced accountability or incompetency.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Doctor, for those of us who may have heard of the concept of post traumatic stress syndrome, that is something completely different from post traumatic psychosis, correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. Post traumatic stress disorder is a condition that has no visible organic reason. It does not fall into the category of psychosis. In the beginning, if you remember, we said that it usually leads either to category one or two accountability. It does not reach the level of psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to continue on now with your description of exogenous mental illness.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Now, we have reached a group of psychotic conditions with a cognitive deficit, and here we have two group patients. One is mental retardation. Mentally retarded persons are those that have never in their life reached a such intellectual level. This is not a case with our subject. It is out of the question, cannot be applied here. And the next category where we see cognitive deficit is a group we call dementia. Dementia are a deterioration of intellectual capacities which means that a person that has at one point reached its intellectual peak and then started deteriorating after that, can dement. So this takes place in a gradual way. We have a strong, mild and minor dementia. Our subject also does not fall into this category. And finally we have a fourth category. These are dependencies. They are quite widespread today in the entire world. One of them is alcoholism. And it can be either something that goes with alcoholism as a diagnosis, a chronic alcoholism, and within that we can also have an acute state of inebriation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you describe for us what are the characteristics of alcoholism without psychoses? Can you describe that for us a bit more?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Alcoholism which, as a rule, has no psychosis but we described alcoholism with psychosis before. Everything else can be described as an urge to have alcohol. A person in the beginning drinks less and then develops dependency, and then once it becomes dependent, then we meet a description that the subject used for himself. When he started drinking, he had a need to drink more. In the beginning when he started drinking, this need was not very strong, and as it grew, then he channelled all of his activities in the direction of obtaining more drinks. In the beginning, he frequently got drunk, but alcoholism as a diagnostic category, as it progresses, the person loses all realistic criteria and can get inebriated more frequent. During that time, the person will develop his or her own state of habits and we call this -- we have a special name for this in psychiatry. That person does not change right away. That person becomes more merry when in company, is usually popular but, however, with time, certain social norms become neglected. Alcoholism can leave consequences in a number of organs, mostly gastrointestinal system, liver. Today we know for sure that there are specific markers that can confirm chronic alcoholism. So what I said about schizophrenia, that we have no indicators for that illness, does not apply here. With alcoholism, we can find a number of indicators. There is an enzyme produced by liver that is usually increased. There are very frequent neurological changes that can be described as goose bumps, then pain in lower extremities. Those are usual symptoms we meet in alcoholism.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, before we conclude your discussion of the different classifications, there are some other classifications that we do not need to go into because they are not relevant in this case, but there are some other classifications of mental illness, correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. Here, under item 5, we listed miscellaneous illnesses which fall into other categories but, however, they were not brought up either by the colleague of mine that also did a report, nor has it been mentioned by your side so we did not detail -- we did not belabour that here in our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But Doctor, before I ask you to describe for us the methodology that you followed in your examination and evaluation of Mr. Vasiljevic, can you please just give us the basic principles that a psychiatrist would use in the evaluation of a new patient, where the psychiatrist does not know any history or psychiatric history of the patient?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: What we see here on this list is a school case example of how a psychological state is determined. What we need to say is that we as forensic psychiatrists are also serving as clinical psychiatrists because the methodology that we use is a psychiatric one. And it is also something that we do in order to answer your question, which is to describe accountability. Psychiatry, just like other medical branches, is a profession and a science which classifies the results of its work within diagnosis. We say also that diagnosis is a base for determining accountability. And in our daily clinical work, diagnosis is something that we use in order to determine therapy. So this is why we could say that the objective of our expertise is to establish a diagnosis which, afterwards, would follow by determination of therapy, prognosis, determination of accountability and so on. Other things you might inquire about is ability to stand trial, recommendation that we could give to the patient, and so on. I as a forensic psychiatrist can also, upon finding that the patient has another illness, will say that the patient needs to be treated for another illness. So this is how we would reach the diagnosis. First of all, we need to determine anamnesis or the history, medical history. This is what in psychiatry is established based on the interview with the patient and acquiring of various information, family information, any family illnesses, pregnancy, labour, whether it was complicated or not, early childhood, whether the patient was social, friendly, and so on, all the way up until today. So we go through the whole life of the patient, regardless of whether something that we are called to establish took place yesterday or ten years ago. Why is it so? Because we have excluding and including methods. Inclusive methods are those that lead us to find symptoms that would confirm the diagnosis, but if we find symptoms of something else, then we would excludes this diagnosis and continue on with our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, can I take from your answer that the term "anamnesis" refers to the personal history that a psychiatrist would take from the person who they are evaluating? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: That's right, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would the psychiatrist believe or assume that every fact given by the patient is true and accurate or would they attempt to determine with other evidence whether or not the patient has given true and accurate information?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a heteroanamnesis. When we as forensic psychiatrists work with patients, then what we usually see is that the patients tell the whole truth because they come to see the doctor in order for the doctor to help them. So when we train our students and psychiatrists in forensic psychiatry, then the most difficult part is to teach them how to discern what information is a truthful one. That is actually a skill.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, can you tell us what the term heteroanamnesis means?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Well, this is how we reach the next degree, which is a heteroanamnesis, and that is a verification of information which patient gave us from somebody else, or perhaps this is something that the patient himself did not remember and we obtained from another person. Most often that other person is a spouse, parents, children of the patient, colleagues from work, friends, classmates, et cetera. So somebody who knows the patient well is a very good person for providing heteroanamnestic information. This kind of information can be usually very important when we have an acutely psychotic person that can give no information on him or herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to anamnesis and heteroanamnesis, what else would you customarily evaluate or look at when evaluating a patient?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Whether we evaluate the patient, then every medical documentation is of great importance to us if it can tell us what is the medical history of the patient. It is also important with respect to mental illnesses and physical ones. What we in psychiatry consider to be most important is listed under item 4, which is the patient's status. This status includes both physical and psychological one. Physical status, something that we in psychiatry consider to be sine qua non, where we base on the facial expressions psychomotoric of the patient his line of thoughts, his emotional state, his total cognitive intellectual mnestic functions, together with anamnestic information, will lead to us determine diagnosis. Psychological status in psychiatry is considered to be a base for establishing diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, can you please first spell the word mnestic and ask you describe what that means? You used the word "mnestic" and can you describe what that means? You used the word "mnestic" function.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: In psychiatry, we divide or we say that everything that is a product of our brain is a cognitive side and those cognitive functions can be divided into intellectual and mnestic ones. Mnestic ones refer to the ability to remember and retain information that we remember. So that is actually ability to intake new facts and retain them. It is very important with patients that suffer from dementia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask you to spell that word in English so the reporters can correctly record it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Mnestic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that might be in B/C/S. Have we got it anywhere in this document or in the doctor's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's in the report, Your Honour, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps so that the court reporters can get it right from the wording, can you look it up?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I can show it. Yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: M-n-e-s-t-i-k?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now, Doctor, what role do psychological tests play in the evaluation of a patient?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Psychological testing is a routine method, in psychiatric evaluation. However, it is not also mandatory testing for all categories. Psychological testing would help in order to describe the personality of the subject. Psychological methods are something that can be used to assess the level of aggression easier. Psychological testing can also help us establish which facts were not truthful. However, when evaluating a subject, psychological testing used -- psychological testing is something that is not entirely precise, that can tell us what is more likely. This testing can tell you that it is very likely that this person has this personality or that personality but this testing cannot determine with certainty what the personality exactly is. What is very important is the following: Had I found that the subject or had I doubts that the subject suffered mental retardation or dementia that could lead to a change in his accountability, then I would call you up and say, "I'm sorry, I cannot reach a conclusion without psychological testing." So in order to evaluate cognitive deterioration, we need a psychologist. I don't need a psychologist once I see that cognitive functions are okay. For example, in my interview with my subject, we started off with some basic questions, where are we, what the date is and so on, and then I said, "Can you please tell me what 100 minus 7 is," and then I can measure the speed, et cetera, of his answer. Then he told me 93. And then we continued until I was sure that his cognitive functions were all right. The subject also defined certain specific concepts and certain abstract Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. concepts to me. So psychiatry has a sufficient area of methods in order to establish whether the person has a disorder or not. However, if the person has a disorder, then we need psychological testing in order to establish what level of disorder there is. So this is all I can tell you about psychological testing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you testifying or telling us that, based upon your initial interview with Mr. Vasiljevic, that you determined that additional psychological testing would not be necessary for you to answer the question that was put to you regarding Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: I would say that I -- it wasn't necessary to me. I didn't find anything that I could not have solved without psychological testing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the role that routine laboratory tests would play in the evaluation of a patient?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. If we have a demented patient, then it is very important to look for the level of B 12 vitamin to see whether there is an insufficiency of it. If I were to establish that the subject was demented, then I would need a CT scan. So we never use routinely magnetic resonance but only when we have a clinical picture that would require this. It is important to run a routine lab test because we need always to determine whether this medication is appropriate or not. What is important with this subject is that his GT levels, gamma GT levels were increased, and this was a further confirmation of my clinical conclusion that he was a chronic alcoholic. So we do run a routine lab test, and then based on clinical picture and symptoms, we determine the other factors that we need to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you to tell us with specificity the different diagnostic steps that you took in your examination of Mr. Vasiljevic. I would ask you at this stage just please to list them and perhaps, after the break, we will begin to go into each of the different steps that you took. Okay? So please just list the different steps that you took.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: I here listed my work method in seven items. First of all, I used information I gained from the documents provided to me by you, by the Tribunal. I read it in detail and I attempted to gain as much as I could from them. The second step was a part of psychiatric evaluation which is a detailed anamnesis and it was a pleasure to work with this subject in that area because he was a very cooperative subject. I then proceeded to determine his present status. His physical status was not of great importance because it had no great impact on his psychological status. I also researched the existing documentation of this subject from the detention unit in Scheveningen, which means that I had the results of lab tests and also information on his therapy from the day he arrived in Scheveningen to the day we held an interview. And finally, I also looked into the opinion by Dr. Lopicic, who is a psychiatrist and who was the first one to provide her expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would ask you just before we break, can you describe for us what you have as number 7, the most important aspect of the diagnosis or determining a diagnosis of Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: The most important, in fact, is that we, in addition to anamnestic information, recognise and assess symptoms or indicators in the subject that are key elements in order to determine diagnosis. I can claim with certainty that what I have seen in this subject and what are used in order to determine diagnosis, was based primarily on the documentation provided to me by the Tribunal but also on the methods of the clinical psychiatrist who has an experience of including and including certain information and relevant knowledge, which means that this is what we have. We saw the patient, we provide a diagnosis, and in order to diagnose the patient retroactively, I used documentation and also indicators of life-long diagnosis, which is something that helped me when using the methods of exclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to ask you to explain a little bit further -- in a little bit greater detail something you said just before the break. You used the term indicators of life-long diagnoses. Would I be correct in saying that indicators would include both symptoms and signs?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please describe for us what are symptoms?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Symptoms are clinical signs which the patient experiences subjectively and which must be recognised by a trained expert. For example, if someone has hallucinations, we shall see that his attention is removed from the subject we are discussing and that the patient is actually hallucinating. If I put a question to the patient, for example, and I see that the patient does not understand me, I will repeat my question and see whether his attention is disturbed or whether his whole system of understanding is disrupted. These are symptoms which are very significant for the establishing of a psychiatric diagnosis. If a patient is talking to me, I tell him to stick to a certain subject but he leaps from topic to topic, for me this is a significant symptom for the recognition of his mental illness. Signs, on the other hand, are for example whether someone has tremour or whether his hands are trembling. That would be a sign because both lay person and a professional will notice it, but a professional will notice whether only the fingers are trembling, whether the hand is trembling only when the patient is still or when he reaches out to take a cup of coffee. A professional will distinguish several categories in this trembling, each of which is specific to a particular diagnosis. A symptom is subjective, a sign is objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the treatment of a person with a diagnosed mental illness, would it be important for the psychiatrist treating that person to record somewhere the symptoms that they learned from the patient?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. It's our duty to do so. We have to document the reason why we are prescribing a certain medicine. In medicine, if something has not been written down, it has not been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: This means excuse me, this means that if someone is delirious, I give him Meprobamate but I did not write it down, tomorrow I will be held responsible if that patient dies as if I had not administered the drug at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd ask you just to say the name of the drug again and spell it for the people transcribing what you're saying? A.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's spelled M-e-p-r-o-b-a-m-a-t; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Sorry, the third from the end is an "M".

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. Now, Doctor, in trying to evaluate what the psychic condition of a person was at a time previously, and that -- I'm sorry, the task is to determine what a person's psychic history was at a previous period in time and in your anamnesis the patient describes for you having certain symptoms, such as certain hallucinations or certain different disturbances of thinking, would it be important to determine whether or not at the time they were treated for that illness, whether or not the treating psychiatrist recorded those symptoms?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: You see, in forensic psychiatry, this is very important, because if someone was psychotic, in the former Yugoslavia, these persons were always hospitalised, and if I want to establish with certainty that this happened, I have to ask why he was not hospitalised, because psychoses were always treated in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. But one of the diagnostic tasks that you describe for us was to examine the history as provided by the patient against other independent information to determine whether it's true and accurate, correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So part of that process would be to ascertain if symptoms reported by the patient were observed by other people back at the time they were treated for that illness, correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you've described the method that you used in examining Mr. Vasiljevic. Did you examine Mr. Vasiljevic and did you write a report regarding his condition?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would like to tender three documents: Prosecution document 168, which is the Serbo-Croatian version, the original version, of the doctor's report; document 168.1, which is the English translation of that report; and document 173, an English version of the Doctor's CV provided by the Doctor herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You've got the B/C/S version of the CV?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Should that be in evidence, the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's available here, Your Honour, and we can certainly introduce it. The English version, Your Honour, was not a translation but one provided by the doctor. That's why I wasn't entirely sure we needed to put in both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, at this stage we will only put the English one in. Exhibit 168 will be the B/C/S version of the doctor's report. What was the date of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a minute, Your Honour, the date of the report is the 17th of December, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit 168.1 -- sorry, P168.1 will be the English translation of that report. Exhibit P173 will be the English translation of the witness's curriculum vitae. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I'd like at this point in time to return to the different types of mental illness or psychoses that you've described for us and could you -- if you would name them for us and then describe for us your findings after your evaluation of Mr. Vasiljevic. And I would ask you to begin with the endogenous or functional psychoses.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: As you can see here, we use the same order as was the order in the classification. We will begin with endogenous or functional psychosis. The first of these is schizophrenia. Based on a detailed examination, a discussion of previous symptoms, an inspection of all previous medical documents for three hospitalisations and an inspection of the therapy administered in Scheveningen, I found no indication that Mr. Vasiljevic ever suffered from schizophrenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you examined the medical records of Mr. Vasiljevic in the detention centre, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And there is a psychiatrist assigned to the patients at the detention centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Vera Popovic, whom I know personally. She is a consulting psychiatrist in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is she is psychiatrist in good standing in the Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: She is a very good psychiatrist in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After examining the medical records from the detention centre, were you able to determine whether or not Mr. Vasiljevic is currently receiving any medication for schizophrenia?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to do this, and to ascertain that Mr. Vasiljevic is not receiving any antipsychotic therapy, either for schizophrenia or paranoid psychosis or affective psychosis. Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic now and several months before my examination, has not been receiving any drugs used to treat any mental illness or disorder. A special group of drugs are used for psychosis, antipsychotics. Throughout the time of his stay in Scheveningen, Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic never received antipsychotics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe you told us before that schizophrenia is a life psychosis. Can we take from that that if Mr. Vasiljevic suffered from schizophrenia in 1992, that at present, he should be receiving some medication for that condition even today?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. He should be receiving medication but I can say, with certainty, that nowhere in any of the documents or in my conversation with him or in his psychic status, nowhere have I found anything to indicate that Mr. Vasiljevic may be suffering from schizophrenia. And this includes the fact that he is not receiving any therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if by some mistake, he was not receiving the appropriate drugs, would you expect to see some symptoms of schizophrenia in Mr. Vasiljevic today?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Yes. Because he has been in detention for two years now, the period is too long for schizophrenic patient to remain in remission without therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, in your practice and your experience, have you ever come across exceptions to this principal that you are now describing for us, that in life psychosis we must always see either therapy, medication for the disease, or illness, or symptoms of the illness? Have you ever seen an exception to that principle?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Never both. I have never seen anyone who had schizophrenia who lived for ten years without either symptoms or signs or therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you now, the next category of psychoses, paranoid psychoses, and what were you able to determine regarding whether Mr. Vasiljevic did or did not have paranoid psychoses back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: As in the case of schizophrenia, I can assert that no description of an event, no anamnestic datum, no symptom or sign or therapy, have awakened a suspicion in me that Mr. Vasiljevic may be suffering from paranoid psychosis. During his two years of detention in Scheveningen, he never received any drugs which are used to treat paranoid psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you now to answer the same question regarding affective psychoses.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: My answer is identical in the case of affective psychosis, all the more so as the frequency of changes in the disorder is even greater than is the case with schizophrenic and paranoid episodes. That is why in modern psychiatry, apart from drugs to treat affective psychosis, so-called stabilisers of moods are also used, the function of which is not only to treat symptoms but also to protect the patient or rather to prevent the symptoms from reappearing. I might say that it is almost the duty of the psychiatrist looking after the patient to continuously administer stabilisers of moods to a person who is suffering from affective psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, before we move to exogenous psychoses, I want to ask you the same question regarding paranoid psychosis and affective psychosis that I asked you about schizophrenia: In your practice and experience, have you ever come across an exception to the principle that you've described here?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I'd ask you to move to your evaluation of Mr. Vasiljevic regarding the exogenous or symptomatic psychoses.

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: When talking of exogenous psychosis, we are entering into an area which is relevant in the case of Mr. Vasiljevic. On the basis of my conversation, my interview with him and the anamnestic data and the symptoms and signs, I endeavoured to establish a diagnosis for the period that he spent in hospital several days after he broke his leg. We now arrive at the fact that my primary diagnosis is delirium. I based this diagnosis mainly on the medical documentation and only then on what I was able to obtain from the gentleman. Then and today, I feel that in the days after he broke his leg, he was suffering from delirium.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, I think perhaps the best way for us to proceed, if we can go through the different illnesses and let's identify those illnesses which you found or determined that he did not have and then we will spend a significant amount of time on your diagnosis regarding the illnesses that you found he may have had, okay?

utterances.speaker: VERA FOLNEGOVIC-SMALC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Alcoholic psychosis, can you just summarise in a sentence or two your findings regarding that?
